title: HOW CAN SCRIPTURE CONDEMN PROSTITUTION YET HONOR RAHAB’S FAITH?
paragraphs: HOW CAN SCRIPTURE CONDEMN PROSTITUTION YET HONOR RAHAB’S FAITH?

The Bible Never Pretended Rahab Was Innocent. It Did Something Far More Shocking—It Put a Prostitute in the Hall of Faith, Brought Her Into the People of God, and Wrote Her Name Into the Family Line of Jesus Christ.
There is a woman in the Bible whose story should make every religious person uncomfortable.
Not because Scripture excuses what she did.
Not because God suddenly changed His mind about sexual sin.
Not because prostitution somehow became righteous.
But because God looked at a woman whose reputation could have followed her to the grave...
and He refused to let her reputation write the final sentence of her life.
And if you have ever wondered whether the worst chapter of your life has disqualified you from being used by God, you may need her story more than you realize.
Because Scripture does something astonishing with Rahab.
It tells us what she was.
It does not sanitize her history.
It does not quietly edit the embarrassing part out.
It does not give her a respectable religious résumé before allowing her into the story.
Joshua 2:1 describes her with the Hebrew expression אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה — ishah zonah — a woman who was a prostitute.
Centuries later, the New Testament does not hide it either.
Two realities that many religious minds would never put in the same sentence.
Not because prostitution ceased to be sin.
But because sin does not possess a greater power to condemn than God possesses to redeem.
Scripture never honors Rahab for prostitution.
And that means the apparent contradiction disappears.
The Bible can condemn prostitution while honoring Rahab for the same reason it can condemn adultery while still speaking of David as a man whose life was profoundly used by God.
For the same reason it can condemn violent persecution while transforming Saul the persecutor into Paul the apostle.
For the same reason Peter can deny Christ and later preach Christ.
God's grace does not require God to call evil good.
Grace does something infinitely more beautiful.
Grace calls sinners out of darkness.
There is an enormous difference between saying, “Your sin is acceptable,” and saying, “Your sin does not have to own you anymore.”
And perhaps this is exactly where Rahab's story stops being merely ancient history and begins invading ours.
Because maybe you have never sold your body.
But perhaps you sold something else.
Your conscience for one more secret night nobody was supposed to know about.
Maybe your scandal does not look like Rahab's.
A browser history you would panic if someone opened.
An abortion you have never told anyone about.
A season when you walked so far from God that even now you sometimes wonder whether you have any right to come home.
And somewhere inside you is a sentence you have been terrified to say aloud:
If people really knew me, would they still believe God could use me?
Because grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
Look at the New Testament's language about sexual immorality.

Paul writes that the body is not meant for sexual immorality but for the Lord. He asks whether the members of Christ should be joined to a prostitute and answers with the strongest possible rejection. Then comes the command:
“δοξάσατε δὴ τὸν θεὸν ἐν τῷ σώματι ὑμῶν.”
Because believers were “bought with a price.”
Christianity therefore does not solve Rahab's story by lowering God's standard.
It solves Rahab's story through redemption.
Sin mattered so much that Christ went to the cross...
and God loved sinners so much that Christ went willingly.
That is why the cross is simultaneously horrifying and beautiful.
It tells us our rebellion is worse than we wanted to admit.
And God's mercy is greater than we dared to imagine.
Everyone had heard what Israel's God had done.
But fear alone did not save Rahab.
Listen to what this Canaanite woman confessed about Israel's God:
“כִּי יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם הוּא אֱלֹהִים בַּשָּׁמַיִם מִמַּעַל וְעַל־הָאָרֶץ מִתָּחַת”
Ki YHWH Eloheikhem hu Elohim bashamayim mimma'al ve'al-ha'aretz mittachat.
“For the LORD your God, He is God in heaven above and on the earth beneath.”
While her city remained opposed to the God of Israel, this woman put her life on the line because she had become convinced that Israel's God was the true God.
Her faith was not merely an emotion.
That is why James later reaches all the way back into Israel's history and brings Rahab forward as an example of living faith:
James points to her receiving the messengers and sending them out safely as evidence of faith demonstrated through action.
He is showing us what genuine faith looks like when it becomes visible.
And Hebrews sees the same thing:
By faith Rahab did not perish with those who remained disobedient.
That may be the two-word sermon somebody reading this desperately needs tonight.
Because some people have been trying to become clean enough to approach Jesus when the Gospel has been telling them to approach Jesus so He can make them clean.
But if sinners could make themselves worthy before coming to Christ, Calvary would have been unnecessary.
You do not wash yourself before taking a bath.
And you do not cure yourself before going to the Physician.
You come because you need Him.
Rahab's story does not tell sinners to become comfortable in sin.
It tells sinners that there is somewhere to run.
But there is something even more breathtaking hidden inside Rahab's story.
The walls that looked permanent collapsed.
The woman society might have considered disposable survived.
Joshua 6 records that Rahab and her family were spared, and Rahab came to live among Israel.
She did not merely receive evacuation from judgment.
The woman marked by her past was incorporated among the covenant people.
And then Scripture takes the story somewhere almost scandalously beautiful.
Matthew opens his Gospel with the genealogy of Jesus Christ.
Ancient genealogies could communicate ancestry, inheritance, legitimacy and identity.
inside the genealogy leading toward Jesus...
Matthew 1:5 identifies Rahab in the ancestral line through Boaz, Obed, Jesse and eventually David, in the genealogy that culminates in Jesus the Messiah.
The woman once known as a prostitute in doomed Jericho appears in the genealogy through which Matthew introduces the Messiah.
God did not erase the fact that she had a past.
He gave her a future her past could never have predicted.
And maybe that is why her story hurts so beautifully.
Because human beings are extraordinarily good at freezing people inside their worst moments.
We turn someone's darkest chapter into the title of their entire book.
But Jesus has always been dangerous to labels.
People saw a Samaritan woman with a shattered relationship history.
Jesus saw someone worth meeting beside a well.
People saw a thief dying beside Him.
Jesus saw a man who would be with Him in paradise.
Jesus saw the shepherd he would become.
But scandal did not get the last word.
And this is where we must be careful, because modern Christianity sometimes mutilates grace in two opposite directions.
One side wants holiness without mercy.
It knows how to expose people but not restore them.
It remembers what someone did ten years after God has transformed them.
It enjoys identifying sin more than seeing sinners reconciled to Christ.
The other side wants mercy without holiness.
It renames sin so nobody feels uncomfortable.
It wants Jesus as Savior without Jesus as Lord.
Jesus does not say your chains are beautiful.
Jesus does not tell you darkness is light.
He brings you into the light.
Jesus does not save us so that we can peacefully remain enslaved to the very things from which He came to redeem us.
Paul's words to the Corinthians are devastatingly hopeful.
After naming patterns of sin, he says of believers:
Then comes the language of transformation:
justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
That single word were contains an entire resurrection.
And perhaps someone reading this is still hiding.
You know when to raise your hands.
But there is a locked room inside your soul where you keep the thing you hope nobody ever discovers.
And you have confused secrecy with safety.
Look how far He came for you.
Rahab's story does not give you permission to remain where you are.
It gives you permission to believe that God can lead you somewhere else.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the God who is calling you home.
And saving faith is not merely agreeing that God exists.
Jericho knew something powerful was happening.
Rahab entrusted herself to the God she had come to believe was Lord of heaven and earth.
That is why her story should disturb both the self-righteous and the hopeless.
The people you have written off may be closer to the kingdom than you imagine.
The thing you did does not possess sovereign authority over the thing God can make of you.
To the sexually broken it says:
Your body does not have to remain a marketplace for someone else's desire. In Christ, you were made for something holier.
Being fully known by God is not the end of hope.
Be very careful whom you consider unusable.
You might be staring at a future testimony.
You might be condemning someone God intends to restore.
You might be looking at a Rahab before the rest of her story has been written.
And to every person secretly thinking, But you don't understand what I've done...
The cross was not designed for respectable people who needed minor improvements.
At Calvary, Jesus did not merely offer inspirational advice.
Forgiveness therefore is not God shrugging at evil.
Christ paid what sinners could never pay.
That is why nobody gets to boast.
We stand beneath the same cross with empty hands.
And there is room there for prostitutes.
There is room for religious hypocrites.
There is room for wounded people who became wounders.
There is room for people who knew better and did it anyway.
There is room for people carrying things they have never told another human being.
Jesus welcomes sinners not because sin is harmless...
but because His blood is sufficient.
He receives us as we are, but His purpose is never to abandon us as we are.
Grace makes old identities surrender to a new Lord.
And this is why Rahab is not evidence that God tolerates prostitution.
Rahab is evidence that prostitution could not prevent a repentant believer from being received into God's redemptive purposes.
God did not honor her prostitution.
And He transformed the trajectory of her life.
That is infinitely better than pretending nothing was wrong.
The world sometimes says, “Never be ashamed of anything.”
“You can bring what is shameful into the light and receive mercy.”
The world says, “This is simply who you are.”
Jesus says your past does not have to be your master.
The world can change your label.
And maybe that is why you found this article.
Not so you could win an argument about Rahab.
Maybe God is confronting the Jericho inside you.
The identity you built around surviving without Him.
And somewhere inside those walls, faith is beginning to whisper:
If that is happening, do not silence it.
Stop negotiating with the thing that is killing your fellowship with God.
There is mercy at the cross.
There is a new way to live.
There is grace strong enough to tell the truth about your past without allowing your past to become your god.
And Christian, if you already belong to Jesus but you have fallen again...
stop using grace as permission to hide.
Confess where confession is biblically appropriate.
Cut off what keeps dragging you back.
Run from sexual immorality instead of negotiating with it.
You were bought with a price.
Maybe your testimony will never sound clean enough for religious people.
Her old designation remained visible in Scripture itself.
Yet Hebrews 11 still placed her among examples of faith.
That should tell you something extraordinary about grace.
God does not need to falsify your history to redeem your future.
He can tell the truth about what happened...
and still write something beautiful afterward.

You do not have to explain everything publicly. You do not owe strangers the private details of your wounds. But sometimes four honest words are the first crack in a wall shame has spent years constructing.
Not merely because sharing helps this ministry reach farther—although it truly does—but because somewhere in your circle may be a Rahab sitting silently behind walls.
Someone who believes church is for people cleaner than them.
Someone one night away from giving up.
Someone who needs to discover that Christianity does not offer permission to remain in sin.
Because the enemy has a cruel way of resurrecting accusations God has already answered with the Gospel, and there may come a night when you need to read this again and remember:
Your worst chapter is not your Savior.
Scripture does not give us permission to make that claim.
Salvation is God's gift in Jesus Christ, and grace cannot be purchased.

If you want to glorify God through your resources, do it first with a surrendered heart and according to Scripture—and if Gospel Warrior is a ministry you prayerfully believe is worth supporting, we would be deeply grateful for you to stand with us.
And there is another reason to stay close.
Because perhaps somebody scrolling tonight does not need another argument.
They need to discover that Scripture can call sin what it is without declaring the sinner beyond redemption.
They need to see a prostitute called to faith.
A shame-filled past unable to prevent a grace-filled future.
Redeemed inside a story ultimately pointing toward Jesus Christ.
How can Scripture condemn prostitution yet honor Rahab's faith?
Because Christianity has never taught that sinners must first have spotless histories before God can save them.
Scripture condemns prostitution because God is holy.
Scripture honors Rahab's faith because God is merciful.
Her past was not called righteous.
God's grace was shown powerful enough to give her a different future.
And that is exactly what the Gospel still does.
It does not rewrite evil and call it good.
So when shame whispers your old name tonight...
When someone reduces you to what you once did...
When the enemy tells you God could never use somebody with your history...
And when you are tempted to look at another broken human being and decide they are simply too filthy, too compromised, too sexually broken, too disgraced, too far gone for Jesus...
Because somewhere between the house in Jericho and the genealogy of the Messiah stands one of the most beautiful truths in all of Scripture:
God can acknowledge every ugly sentence in your past without allowing any of them to become the final sentence of your life.
The walls may remember who you were.
People may remember what you did.
Shame may keep calling you by yesterday's name.
But when Jesus takes hold of a surrendered life, yesterday may explain where you came from—it no longer gets to decide where grace is taking you.
